problem: Source states two alternatives ("either a commercial undertaking is to be managed, or some speculation ... to be tried"); candidate introduces an unsupported hedge "Perhaps".
replacement: There is only one country on earth where citizens enjoy unlimited freedom of association for political purposes. This same country is the only one in the world where the constant exercise of the right of association has been carried into civil life, and where all the advantages that civilization can offer are obtained through it. In every country where political associations are forbidden, civil associations are rare. It is hardly likely that this is an accident. We should rather infer that there is a natural, and perhaps a necessary, connection between these two kinds of associations. Certain men happen to share an interest in some matter. Either a commercial undertaking is to be managed, or some manufacturing venture is to be tried. They meet and combine, and in this way they gradually become familiar with the principle of association. The more numerous the small affairs are, the more men acquire, without even knowing it, the skill to carry out great undertakings together. Civil associations therefore make political association easier. But political association, on the other hand, remarkably strengthens and improves associations for civil purposes. In civil life every man may, strictly speaking, imagine that he can provide for his own needs. In politics he can imagine nothing of the kind. When a people has any knowledge of public life, then, the idea of association and the wish to unite occur every day to the whole community. Whatever natural reluctance may keep men from acting together, they will always be ready to combine for the sake of a party. Political life thus makes the love and practice of association more general. It gives a desire for union, and teaches the means of combining, to numbers of men who would otherwise have lived apart all their lives.

problem: Awkward, unnatural English: "It is equally one to suppose that" (a dangling pronoun for "unrealistic fantasy").
replacement: It is therefore an unrealistic fantasy to suppose that the spirit of association, when it is suppressed on one point, will still show the same vigor on all others. It is just as unrealistic to suppose that if men are allowed to pursue certain undertakings in common, that is enough to make them take them up eagerly. When the members of a community are allowed and accustomed to combine for all purposes, they will combine as readily for the smaller ones as for the more important. But if they are allowed to combine only for small affairs, they will be neither inclined nor able to do it. It is in vain that you leave them entirely free to carry on their business as joint-stock companies. They will hardly care to use the rights you have granted them. And after you have exhausted your strength in vain efforts to put down the prohibited associations, you will be surprised that you cannot persuade men to form the associations you encourage.

problem: Hedge dropped: source says political associations "tend amazingly to multiply and facilitate" civil ones; candidate states it as a flat fact.
replacement: This naturally leads me to think that freedom of association in political matters is not as dangerous to public tranquility as is supposed. It may even be that, after stirring up society for some time, it strengthens the state in the end. In democratic countries, political associations are, so to speak, the only powerful persons who aspire to rule the state. The governments of our time accordingly look on such associations as the sovereigns of the Middle Ages looked on the great vassals of the crown. They feel a kind of instinctive abhorrence of them and combat them on every occasion. They feel, on the contrary, a natural goodwill toward civil associations, because they readily see that these institutions, instead of directing the minds of the community toward public affairs, divert them from such reflections. By engaging men more and more in the pursuit of objects that cannot be attained without public tranquility, civil associations deter them from revolutions. But these governments overlook the fact that political associations tend amazingly to multiply and ease those of a civil character, and that in avoiding a dangerous evil they deprive themselves of an effective remedy.

problem: Causal connective lost: source "But since the imagination takes less lofty flights ... moralists are alarmed"; candidate "Now the imagination ..." makes it a bare juxtaposition.
replacement: When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, these people liked to hold a lofty idea of the duties of man. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as God himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that time. I doubt whether men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others. But they talked ceaselessly about the beauty of virtue, and they studied its usefulness only in private. But now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man’s thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by this idea of self-sacrifice, and they no longer dare to offer it to the human mind. They content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not lie in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are eager to bring it to notice. Observations of this kind gradually multiply. What was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held to be true that man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.
